section.title: Make a Joyful Noise to the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The shortest and best known of the enthronement psalms, this five-verse hymn of thanksgiving closes the sequence begun in Psalm 93 with a universal summons to joyful, grateful worship grounded in the LORD's identity as Maker and Shepherd and His goodness that endures to every generation.
section.thesis: Because the LORD is God, our Maker and Shepherd, and because He is good, His loving devotion and faithfulness enduring forever, all the earth is summoned to enter His presence with joyful songs and thanksgiving.
section.frameNote: Two cycles of command and reason: a call to joyful, grateful worship because the LORD made us and we are His, verses 1-3; and a call to thankful entry into His presence because He is good and everlastingly faithful, verses 4-5.

units.label: Know that the Lord is God
units.note: a call to joyful worship of our Maker

verses.text: A Psalm of thanksgiving. Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth.
Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs.
{{yada|Know}} that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture.

units.label: His loving devotion endures forever
units.note: a call to thankful entry into His presence

verses.text: Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise; give thanks to Him and bless His name.
For the LORD is good, and His {{chesed|loving devotion}} endures forever; His faithfulness continues to all generations.

yada.gloss: To know intimately, not merely intellectually. Knowing that the LORD is God grounds all true worship in settled fact rather than fleeting feeling, an intimate acknowledgment of who made us and to whom we belong.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love. This word anchors Israel's whole understanding of God's character, His love that does not depend on human performance but endures forever, fully revealed in Christ's own steadfast love for His people.

basic.context: This short psalm of thanksgiving gathers up the enthronement sequence of Psalms 93-99 into a five-verse invitation: know that the LORD is God, our Maker and Shepherd, and therefore enter His presence with joyful songs and grateful praise, because His goodness and faithfulness never run out.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's global address, 'all the earth,' functions as a genuine summons to every people, not poetic flourish, resting on the same truth Genesis 1 and Israel's covenant both affirm, that the God who made all people is worthy of worship from all people.
basic.originalLanguages: To yada, know, that the LORD is God is more than intellectual assent, it is intimate, settled acknowledgment of His identity as Maker and Shepherd. His chesed, loving devotion, is the steadfast, covenant love that endures forever and anchors the psalm's closing confidence.
basic.typology: The image of God's people as 'the sheep of His pasture' anticipates Jesus' own words, 'I am the good shepherd... I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,' John 10:11, 14, showing that the intimate care this psalm celebrates finds its fullest expression in Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus identifies Himself directly with this psalm's shepherd imagery when He declares, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and the psalm's call for 'all the earth' to enter God's gates with thanksgiving anticipates the ingathering of every nation into worship of God through Christ, fulfilling the psalm's universal scope.
basic.god: God is Maker, the one who made us rather than we ourselves, and Shepherd, the one who cares intimately for His people as His own flock, and He is unfailingly good, His loving devotion and faithfulness reaching to every generation without exception.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:11-16 shows Jesus as the good Shepherd who knows His sheep, echoing this psalm's pastoral imagery. Psalm 95:7 shares the same 'sheep of His pasture' language. Hebrews 13:15 calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through Jesus. Revelation 7:9 pictures a multitude from every nation gathered in worship, fulfilling this psalm's universal summons.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's summons for all the earth to know the LORD as Maker and Shepherd and to enter His presence with grateful joy is fulfilled in Christ, the good Shepherd who knows His own, through whom people of every nation are gathered into everlasting thanksgiving before God.

context.literary:
Psalm 100 is five verses long and has the neatest structure in the Psalter. It is two calls to worship, each followed by a reason. Verses 1 and 2 give three commands, make a joyful noise, serve, come, and the ground is given in verse 3, where the first word is itself a command, 'Know,' and what follows is three statements about who the LORD is and who we are. Verse 4 gives three more commands, enter, give thanks, bless, and verse 5 gives the reason with the small word 'for' that opens it. The two halves are then almost symmetrical: each opens with commands to come in with gladness, each closes on a statement about God, and the second statement, about His goodness and enduring love, answers the first, about His making and owning.

Within each half there is a movement from outward act to inward knowledge. The first half begins with noise and ends with knowing. The second begins with gates and ends with the LORD's character. The psalm takes the worshippers from the road to the gate, from the gate to the courts, and from the courts to the truth that makes the approach possible.

The pronouns carry a story of their own. The first verses address 'all the earth' in the plural, 'you.' Then in verse 3 the speaker slides into 'us' and 'we': 'It is He who made us, and we are His.' The voice that began by summoning the world to worship has joined the worshippers. By verse 5 the pronouns are gone and the LORD stands alone, which is how the psalm closes: not with what the worshippers feel, but with His goodness.

The psalm is the last in a sequence that began at Psalm 93, where the refrain 'The LORD reigns' opens the series. It is simple where Psalm 99 was awesome, and warm where Psalm 99 trembled. The two together show the LORD as a holy King to whom the nations kneel and as a Shepherd in whose pasture His people graze. Psalm 100 has no mention of judgment at all. The one truth it leaves the congregation with is that the LORD is good.
context.historical:
The psalm's heading in the Hebrew calls it a psalm 'for thanksgiving,' using the word todah, the same word that names the thank offering in Leviticus 7:12. That offering was a fellowship sacrifice brought by someone who wanted to give thanks for a rescue, and it was eaten in a shared meal with bread, so it was a joyful, communal occasion and not a sombre ritual. The heading suggests that the psalm was sung as worshippers came to the temple with such offerings, and the word todah appears again in verse 4 as the thanksgiving with which the gates are entered.

The picture the psalm draws is a festival procession. The worshippers come to Jerusalem from the countryside, singing, they pass through the gates of the city or of the temple area, and they enter the courts. The pilgrims who sang such songs in groups of family, village and clan had been travelling for days, and the psalm's sequence of shout, enter, give thanks and bless follows the route. Jeremiah mentions 'those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD,' Jeremiah 33:11, singing 'Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever,' which is a cousin of verse 5 and shows that the language of this psalm was stock language of Israel's gatherings.

The shepherd image would have been as familiar to the first hearers as any in their world. Flocks were the wealth of the people. The idea that a people are 'the sheep of His pasture' would have carried a sense of care and ownership together, and it lies behind the address to kings as shepherds in the prophets, as in Jeremiah 23:1. Israel's own self-understanding was of a flock brought out of Egypt and led through the wilderness, Psalm 77:20, and a thankful hymn naturally said so.

The date cannot be fixed. The psalm is undated and its language is timeless, which may explain why it has been so widely used. A people returning from exile would have sung it with new feeling, and so would a village choir in a later century. The psalm says nothing narrow enough to pin it to one occasion, and the openness is part of its power.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws on the whole Bible's vocabulary of creation and covenant, and many later passages draw on it. The claim that 'It is He who made us' echoes the creation of humanity in Genesis 1:26 and 2:7, and the statement that we are His people and the sheep of His pasture echoes the covenant formula of belonging to the LORD. Psalm 95:6 to 7 is a near twin of verse 3: 'the LORD our Maker. For He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care.' Together they suggest that the two psalms were sung as a pair at the approach to worship.

The ending of the psalm is one of the most repeated lines in the Old Testament. 'The LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever' appears in Psalm 106:1, 118:1 and 136:1, in David's song at the ark in 1 Chronicles 16:34, in Solomon's dedication of the temple, 2 Chronicles 5:13 and 7:3, and in the rebuilding of the foundation after the exile, Ezra 3:11. That last passage is telling: when the returned exiles laid the foundation of the second temple, this was the song they sang, so that the thanksgiving of Psalm 100 is also the song of a restored people.

The shepherd theme runs into the prophets, where the LORD is the Shepherd who searches for scattered sheep, Ezekiel 34:11 to 16, and into the Psalter, most famously in Psalm 23:1. In the New Testament, Jesus says 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and 'I am the gate,' John 10:9, which brings together the psalm's two images, the pasture and the gate. The writer to the Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20, and Peter says believers have returned to 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,' 1 Peter 2:25. Revelation promises that 'the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd,' Revelation 7:17.

The call to thanksgiving is also taken into the church's life. Paul tells the Colossians to sing 'with gratitude in your hearts to God,' Colossians 3:16, and Hebrews says believers are to offer 'a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15, which is the thank offering of the psalm's heading translated into the life of the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants to do something modest and deep: to teach a congregation how to come to God. The psalm is an instruction in worship as much as a song of it, and its plan is that a crowd entering the temple would be told, in the act of entering, what they are doing and why. They are not coming to earn a hearing. They come because the LORD is God, because He made them and they belong to Him, and because He is good. The commands in the psalm are all forms of entering with joy, and the order is deliberate: sound first, then service, then gates and courts.

The second aim is to correct any idea that worship is a burden. 'Serve the LORD with gladness' puts serving and gladness in a single phrase. The word for serve can cover labour, ritual service and homage, and the psalm says none of these should be done with a long face. The author wants hearers to see that joy is not an extra but the right posture for someone who knows whose they are.

The third aim is to widen the circle. 'All the earth' is the first audience. The psalmist does not mean that only Israelites are to sing, and the phrase points to the nations being invited into the flock. A local festival procession is given a global horizon.

The fourth aim is to fix the ground of everything in God's character and not the worshipper's mood. The last verse gives three facts about Him, good, enduring in loving devotion, and faithful from one generation to the next, and these do not depend on what kind of week anyone has had. The psalm tells the worshipper to come with joy because these things are true.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This psalm is almost all prescription. Nearly every clause in verses 1, 2, 3 and 4 is a command, and the description of God in verses 3 and 5 is what the commands rest on. So the question for a reader is less whether to apply it than how literally to do so.

The commands about noise, songs, gates and courts are tied to the temple and its procession. Christians do not enter temple gates, and Hebrews says believers have come to the heavenly Zion, Hebrews 12:22. What carries across is not the architecture but the posture: gladness, thanksgiving, praise, and blessing His name. Jesus Himself says worship of the Father will be 'in spirit and truth,' John 4:23.

The psalm also does not prescribe that every worshipper feel cheerful on every occasion. It commands gladness, but the Psalter elsewhere gives whole psalms to lament, and Psalm 100 does not cancel them. The commands are addressed to a congregation, and the gladness is possible because it does not rest on private circumstances. A person who is grieving can still give thanks for who God is and what He has done, and the psalm allows for the joy that is found in the facts.

Verse 3 is description, a statement of what is the case: the LORD is God, He made us, we are His. The commands follow from it, and so does the order of the Christian life. First we are told what is true, and only then are we told what to do.

The sheep image is description of a relationship and not a call to passivity. Scripture uses it to say that God guides and provides, and it says elsewhere that His people are to listen and follow, John 10:27, but it is not a licence for carelessness.

debates.question: In verse 3, do the people say 'and we are His' or 'and not we ourselves'?

views.label: 'We are His'
views.case: The Hebrew reading tradition, the qere, has a word for 'to Him' or 'His' that is read aloud as lo, and the BSB and most modern translations follow it. The sense is ownership and belonging, parallel to 'the people of His pasture' in the next line.

views.label: 'And not we ourselves'
views.case: The written consonants of the Hebrew, the ketiv, give lo in the sense of 'not,' and the BSB notes this in its footnote, 'Or and not we ourselves.' The Greek and Latin versions and the older English versions followed this. On that reading the verse is a declaration that we did not make ourselves, which fits 'It is He who made us' in the line before it.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm the same truth from different angles, that God is Creator and we are creatures. The majority reading adds belonging and care, and the other adds dependence, and neither contradicts the rest of the psalm.

debates.question: What does it mean to 'serve' the LORD in verse 2?

views.label: Temple worship and ritual service
views.case: The verb is used for the work of priests and Levites in the sanctuary and the psalm is set as a procession into the temple courts. The verse then asks that the ritual service of the festival be done with gladness and not as duty.

views.label: Whole life obedience
views.case: The same verb serves for the labour of a servant to a master and is used in Exodus of Israel's service of the LORD, as opposed to service of Pharaoh. On this reading the verse asks for a life of service given with joy, of which the temple procession is one expression.

debates.bearing: The verb is broad enough to hold both, and the psalm's call to come 'into His presence' suggests the first, while the claim that we belong to Him suggests the second. The bearing for the church is that neither ritual nor duty is enough without gladness.

study.originalLanguages:
Six words and features of the Hebrew add something to the English.

First, the opening command, 'make a joyful noise,' is hari'u, from the root rua, which is the same root that gives teruah, the word for the shout or trumpet blast of a festival or a battle. In Psalm 98:4 the same verb is used, and in Numbers 10:10 the trumpets are to sound on the feast days. The word is not a polite hum but a loud, public acclamation of a king. The BSB renders it 'joyful noise,' which rightly keeps the noise. The object is 'to the LORD,' and the audience is 'all the earth,' so the demand is universal.

Second, verse 3 opens with de'u, 'know,' from yada, a verb that in Hebrew covers knowing by experience and acknowledgement, not only information. Elsewhere it describes the knowing of a husband and wife and the knowing of the LORD by those in covenant with Him, so the command is to recognise Him by relationship. The content is given at once: the LORD, YHWH, is Elohim, God. To say this in a world of many gods was a confession, and the statement is placed as the foundation of the psalm's call to worship.

Third, the verbs of making and owning in verse 3 form a pair: 'made us,' asanu, and the claim that we are His. The word asah, to make, is the same verb used of God's creating in Genesis, and so the psalm grounds belonging in creation. The phrase 'the people of His pasture' and 'sheep' come from the vocabulary of shepherding, where the word for pasture refers to the place where the flock is fed and led. The shepherd is owner and provider. The text does not say 'shepherd' directly, but the image is complete in the words 'sheep of His pasture,' and later readers completed it with Psalm 23.

Fourth, the word in verse 4, todah, 'thanksgiving,' is from the root yadah, to give thanks, which also means to confess or to acknowledge openly. The noun is used in the psalm's heading, for the thank offering, and in verse 4 for the spirit in which the gates are entered. Its partner tehillah, 'praise,' gives the Hebrew name of the whole book of Psalms, Tehillim. So the two nouns of verse 4 sum up what the Psalter as a whole is.

Fifth, verse 4 ends with barekhu shemo, 'bless His name.' The verb barak, to bless, in its usual direction is God blessing people. When people bless God, the word means to acknowledge Him as the source of good, to speak well of Him. The 'name' stands for His whole revealed character, so to bless the name is to say aloud what He has shown Himself to be.

Sixth, the last verse uses three descriptions, tov, chesed and emunah. The first is the plain Hebrew word for 'good,' and the Psalter often places it at the head of the praise formula, as in Psalm 136:1. The BSB renders chesed 'loving devotion,' a covenant love that holds fast, and emunah 'faithfulness,' from the root that gives 'amen,' meaning firmness and reliability. The phrase 'to all generations' is literally 'to generation and generation,' ledor vador, a doubling that is a Hebrew way of saying 'without end.' The verb in the second clause is not there in the Hebrew, which has a short, verbless sentence, so the statement is one of settled fact, as though the writer were pointing.

typology.type: The thank offering and the gates of the temple, verses 1 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The todah was the sacrifice of those who came with gratitude for rescue, and worshippers came through the gates to offer it. Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved,' John 10:9, and Hebrews tells believers to 'continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15, through Him. The escalation is that the entrance and the offering are both found in Christ. The type falls short because the gates were physical and the thank offering was animal and grain, while Christ is the gate who opens access to every person and the fruit of lips is now the offering.

typology.type: The flock and its shepherd, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The 'sheep of His pasture' finds its fullest form in Jesus: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. He says He will bring other sheep not of this fold so that there will be one flock and one shepherd, John 10:16, which is the ingathering the psalm's 'all the earth' hints at. Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20, and Revelation 7:17 says the Lamb will shepherd the redeemed. The type falls short in that an ordinary shepherd lives off his flock, while this Shepherd dies for His.

typology.type: The Creator who makes a people, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The Maker of verse 3 becomes the Maker of a new creation. Paul says believers are 'God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works,' Ephesians 2:10, and that anyone in Christ is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17. Peter says that those who were not a people are now the people of God, 1 Peter 2:9 to 10, a chosen people belonging to Him. The type falls short in that the first making gave life to a people already in the womb of history, whereas the new making brings life to the dead, and gathers Gentiles who were once outsiders.

typology.type: Enduring love to all generations, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The promise that His loving devotion and faithfulness last from one generation to the next is first given to a family line, and its clearest form is the promise to David that his throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:13 and 16, with loving devotion that would never be removed. The New Testament sees the promise land on one descendant, Acts 2:30 to 31, and Hebrews says that Christ's priesthood is permanent, Hebrews 7:24. The promise of endless love is thus not left in the air but anchored in a person who lives forever. The type falls short because a human line, even David's, ends in death, and the psalm's 'forever' needs a king who does not.

study.christ:
Psalm 100 has no prophecy in it, and it would be a mistake to look for one. What it has is a set of pictures that the Gospels and the letters pick up and complete in Christ. There are four.

The first is the shepherd. The psalm says we are 'the sheep of His pasture,' and Jesus answers by saying of Himself, 'I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep,' John 10:14 to 15. The LORD whom the psalm calls God and owner of the flock is speaking in the first person. Ezekiel 34 had said that the LORD Himself would search for His scattered sheep, Ezekiel 34:11 to 16, and that He would set one shepherd over them, Ezekiel 34:23, and Jesus gathers the two promises together. In Matthew 9:36 He sees crowds 'like sheep without a shepherd' and is moved with compassion, which shows what the shepherd image meant in His hands: tender, searching care. The difference from any human shepherd is stated plainly, since He lays down His life.

The second is the gate. The psalm's worshippers enter gates and courts with thanksgiving. Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture,' John 10:9. The pasture and the gate are the two pictures of the psalm, and He claims both. The letter to the Hebrews adds that through Him believers may 'approach the throne of grace with confidence,' Hebrews 4:16, so the entry is now not through a stone gate into a courtyard but through a person into the very presence of God.

The third is the flock gathered from every nation. The psalm's opening address to 'all the earth' is more than a wish. Jesus says, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd,' John 10:16. Paul reads the same ingathering when he says Christ has made the two one, and that those who were far away have been brought near, Ephesians 2:13 to 19. The worldwide invitation of Psalm 100 is honoured in the worldwide mission of the church, and Paul's quotation of 'Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles,' Romans 15:11, from Psalm 117, sits next to it.

The fourth is the goodness that endures. The psalm grounds everything in the fact that the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures. The clearest display of that in history is the cross, where God 'demonstrates His own love for us' in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners, Romans 5:8, and the clearest promise is the resurrection, which shows that His love outlives death. The faithfulness that reaches 'to all generations' is the faithfulness that raised Jesus and will raise those who are His.

A caution is in order. The psalm is not about Jesus in the way a prediction is, and the Gospel of John does not say it is. What John does is to show that the God whom the psalm names as Maker and Shepherd has come in person, and that Jesus speaks the very words of the shepherd-God of the Old Testament. The psalm is fulfilled not by being unlocked like a code but by the arrival of the One it was about from the beginning.
study.god:
Psalm 100 gives a God who is worth coming to. It says three things about Him, and each one is a doctrine.

The first is that He is God and we are not. 'Know that the LORD is God' is a short line with large consequences. There is one God, He has a name, and He is the source of the world and of us. This is the basis of monotheism in the Psalter, and it is stated as something to be known, not argued. The psalm then adds 'It is He who made us.' That claim is about dependence: nothing about us is self-made. It is also about dignity, for the Maker of the universe has taken an interest in a people. Creation and covenant are run together in one sentence, and the same God who made all things has made a people His own.

The second is that God is a shepherd. The psalm never uses the word, but 'sheep of His pasture' draws the picture. The God who is beyond the heavens is also the God who feeds, leads, protects and owns. A shepherd in Israel's world was close to his animals, knew them and risked himself for them. The image teaches a doctrine of providence that is personal and not distant, and of ownership that is kind and not exploitative. It also guards against pride, for sheep are not clever.

The third is that God is good, and the goodness is specific. The psalm says His loving devotion endures forever and His faithfulness continues to all generations. Good here is not vague niceness but a covenant commitment that holds. There is a tension to notice. The same God who is 'holy' in Psalm 99 and who 'avenges misdeeds' is the God who is simply 'good' here. The psalms put the two side by side without comment, and the sequence, which passes from the throne of the nations to the pasture of the flock, teaches that holiness and goodness are not rivals. Exodus 34:6 says it all in one breath, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.'

There is another tension: God is the Creator of all the earth and the shepherd of a particular people. The psalm addresses 'all the earth' and then says 'we are His people.' It does not resolve this by making Israel's claim smaller but by making the invitation bigger. The God who owns a people means for the whole earth to be among them.

For worship, this psalm teaches that the reasons for gladness are all in God, and that gladness is the fitting response. Worship starts with knowing, since the first command of verse 3 is to know. It moves to thanks, because everything we have is a gift of our Maker. It reaches to blessing His name, which is the joy of saying aloud what is good about Him. And it lives in confidence, because what is true of Him does not change from one generation to the next. Even a person whose life is hard can stand at the gate of this psalm, because it does not ask them to feel that all is well, only to recall who is God.

crossReferences.note: This psalm says 'let us kneel before the LORD our Maker. For He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care.' It is the nearest parallel to Psalm 100:3, using nearly the same claims of making and shepherding, and the two may have been sung together at the approach to worship.

'The LORD is my shepherd' personalises what Psalm 100:3 says of the whole flock. Psalm 23 has the individual believer speaking, and Psalm 100 has the congregation; together they show that the shepherd-God cares for each sheep by name and for the whole flock.

The LORD says He Himself will search for His flock and seek them out, rescuing the scattered and feeding them on good pasture. This gives the sheep image of Psalm 100:3 its hope for a time when human shepherds had failed, and it is the promise that Jesus takes up in John 10.

The LORD God formed the man from the dust and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. It is the primal account of 'It is He who made us,' and it shows that our existence is a gift of His breath, which is why thanksgiving is the fitting response.

The law of the thank offering requires unleavened cakes with oil along with the sacrifice of thanksgiving. The same Hebrew word, todah, stands in the heading of Psalm 100 and in verse 4, so the psalm puts the spirit of that offering into words for a procession of thankful worshippers.

At the dedication of Solomon's temple the trumpeters and singers joined in praising the LORD with one voice, 'For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever,' and the house was filled with a cloud. The line is Psalm 100:5 in its natural home, sung at the moment when God's presence came to the place the psalm invites people to enter.

When the exiles laid the foundation of the second temple they sang responsively, 'For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever,' and gave a great shout of praise. The psalm's closing confidence was the song of a people rebuilding after ruin, which shows that it is meant to be sung in hard times as well as glad.

'Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever' opens a psalm that repeats the second half of the line in every verse. Psalm 136 shows how much Israel leaned on this sentence, and the repetition there gives the weight of Psalm 100:5.

Jesus says 'I am the gate' and 'I am the good shepherd.' The psalm's two pictures, pasture and gate, are both claimed by Him. The verse about laying down His life shows what the shepherd-God of the psalm would do for His flock.

'Let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.' The writer takes the todah of the psalm and the 'bless His name' of verse 4 and makes them the standing offering of the church, offered through Jesus.

Believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works. This is the new-creation version of 'It is He who made us, and we are His,' and it shows that the claim of Psalm 100:3 is renewed in the gospel.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 100 is small, but it touches every part of the Bible's story because it is built from three of its largest claims: God made us, God owns us, and God is good.

It answers the beginning. Genesis says the LORD God formed the man from dust and breathed life into him, Genesis 2:7, and made humanity in His own image, Genesis 1:26, so that the claim 'It is He who made us' is the first fact about every person. The fall did not cancel it but made it easy to forget. The serpent's question in Genesis 3:1 was precisely about whether God could be trusted to be good, and the psalm is the answer of a people who have learned to say, 'The LORD is good.' Every generation of the Bible has to decide again whether the serpent or the psalm is telling the truth.

It gathers the middle. Israel's rescue from Egypt was the rescue of a flock, and the wilderness years were a shepherd leading sheep, as the Psalter later recalls. The prophets saw the flock scattered by bad shepherds and promised that the LORD Himself would come to gather them, Ezekiel 34:11 to 16. The psalm's sentence 'His loving devotion endures forever' is one of Israel's staple lines: sung at the ark, at the temple's dedication, and at the foundation of the second temple in Ezra 3:11. It served as the people's confession on the day of triumph and on the day of reconstruction after ruin.

It sets up the gospel. Jesus steps into this language and says, 'I am the good shepherd,' and 'I am the gate,' John 10:9 and 11. The Shepherd who was promised arrives, lays down His life and takes up His flock from every nation. The psalm's 'all the earth' becomes the mission of the church, and Paul's quoting of the nations' praise in Romans 15:9 to 11 brings the strand to its natural place. The thank offering of the heading finds its continuation in the sacrifice of praise, Hebrews 13:15.

It ends in the new creation. The last book pictures the redeemed from every tribe and tongue standing before the throne, and the Lamb in the midst of the throne shepherding them, leading them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The gates of Psalm 100 reappear as the gates of the city, and the thanksgiving of the courts has become the song of the whole creation. The 'all generations' of verse 5 has run out, not because His love ended but because the generations have all been gathered in. What the psalm asks the church to do on a Sunday, to come in with gladness, it will do without pause in the world to come.

sermon.title: A Psalm for Giving Thanks
sermon.why: Preached directly on Psalm 100:1-5, as confirmed by the sermon's own scripture reference on truthforlife.org, Begg examines this psalm's call to joyful, thankful worship grounded in the truths of God's Word, showing that entering His gates with praise depends on the redeeming work of the Lord Jesus Christ.

quiz.q: Who is summoned to make a joyful noise to the LORD in verse 1?

options.text: All the earth.
options.note: The psalm's opening summons is explicitly universal in scope, addressed to all the earth.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The summons reaches far beyond the priesthood to all the earth.

options.text: Only the tribe of Levi.
options.note: The call is universal, not limited to a single tribe.

options.text: Only the nation of Israel.
options.note: Israel is certainly included, but the psalm's address explicitly extends to all the earth.

quiz.q: What is the stated reason for worship in verse 3?

options.text: Know that the LORD is God; He made us, and we are His people, the sheep of His pasture.
options.note: Verse 3 grounds worship in the settled knowledge of God's identity as Maker and Shepherd.

options.text: Because Israel has just won a military victory.
options.note: The reason given is God's identity as Creator and Shepherd, not a military victory.

options.text: Because the harvest has been unusually abundant this year.
options.note: The stated reason is theological, God's identity, not agricultural abundance.

options.text: Because the psalmist wants to impress other nations.
options.note: The reason given is grounded in God's own character and identity, not a desire to impress others.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the manner of entering God's presence in verse 4?

options.text: With thanksgiving and praise.
options.note: Verse 4 specifically calls worshipers to enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise.

options.text: With silence and complete withdrawal from speech.
options.note: The psalm calls for thanksgiving and praise, not silence.

options.text: With elaborate sacrificial rituals exclusively.
options.note: The psalm names thanksgiving and praise, not a detailed sacrificial system, as the manner of entry.

options.text: With formal legal petitions only.
options.note: The psalm's language is of thanksgiving and praise, not legal petition.

quiz.q: According to verse 5, how long do the LORD's goodness and faithfulness last?

options.text: His loving devotion endures forever, and His faithfulness continues to all generations.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly states these qualities endure forever and reach every generation.

options.text: Only for the lifetime of the current generation.
options.note: The text explicitly extends God's faithfulness to all generations, not just the current one.

options.text: Only until the next national crisis occurs.
options.note: The psalm presents God's faithfulness as unconditional and enduring, not contingent on the absence of crisis.

options.text: For a limited, specified number of centuries.
options.note: The psalm's language is of permanence, 'forever' and 'to all generations,' not a specified limited period.

quiz.q: How does Jesus take up this psalm's pastoral imagery in the New Testament?

options.text: He declares Himself the good Shepherd who knows His sheep, John 10:11-14.
options.note: Jesus directly applies the shepherd and sheep imagery of this psalm to His own relationship with His people.

options.text: He rejects the shepherd and sheep imagery as inadequate.
options.note: Jesus embraces and fulfills this imagery rather than rejecting it.

options.text: He applies it only to the twelve apostles and no one else.
options.note: Jesus' shepherd imagery in John 10 extends to all His sheep, not the twelve apostles exclusively.

options.text: He applies it exclusively to Israel's ancient kings.
options.note: Jesus applies the shepherd imagery to Himself personally, not merely to Israel's past kings.

questions: This psalm grounds joyful worship in the settled knowledge that 'the LORD is God' rather than in shifting feelings or circumstances. What would change in your own worship this week if it were anchored more firmly in who God is rather than in how you feel?
The psalm calls God's people 'the sheep of His pasture,' an image of complete dependence and care. Where in your life do you resist depending on God as fully as a sheep depends on its shepherd?
Entering God's gates is to be done 'with thanksgiving,' not grudgingly or out of mere obligation. What specific things could you name right now as reasons for genuine thanksgiving before God?

The psalm declares that God's faithfulness continues 'to all generations.' How does trusting God's faithfulness across generations shape the way you think about your own children, grandchildren, or those who will come after you in the faith?
Jesus calls Himself the good Shepherd who knows His sheep by name. How does it change your sense of belonging to know that the Maker of all the earth also knows you personally through Christ?

translationNotes.note: A well known textual variant renders this phrase 'and not we ourselves' rather than 'and we are His,' both readings emphasizing that human beings owe their existence entirely to God rather than to themselves.
The Hebrew word rendered 'joyful noise' (rua) is the same root used elsewhere for a victory shout, indicating exuberant, triumphant praise rather than quiet reflection.

'Loving devotion' renders the Hebrew chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, paired here with 'faithfulness,' emunah, a word elsewhere used of firm, load-bearing pillars, underscoring God's utter reliability.
